## Upgrading from v0.4.0

**Re-lift anything whose symbols could hold a quote, a backslash or a control
character.** The lifting script escaped none of them (#77), so files produced by
v0.4.0 and earlier fall into two cases.

A name holding a `"` produced a file that cannot be parsed at all. If you have
such a file, `extract` has been refusing it with a JSON error naming a line and
column; lifting it again is the fix, and any copy repaired by hand can be
discarded.

A name holding a `\` is the case worth knowing about, because nothing announced
it. The file parses. A name written as `\t` is read back as a name holding a
tab, so the birthmark was extracted from a name the program does not have, and
the similarity it took part in was computed against the wrong string. `fc-*`
birthmarks are built from symbol names and are affected directly; the `op-*`
families do not use names and are not.

Nothing else about the format changed, so files without such names are
unaffected and need not be regenerated. A lift of the same binary before and
after this release is byte-identical unless one of these characters appears.

## Highlights

- **#77** — `lift` escapes the names it writes into the intermediate JSON.
  Nine values reached the file unescaped, so a C++ user-defined literal
  operator — which Ghidra demangles as `operator""__km` — produced a file
  `extract` could not read, while `lift` itself exited 0 and reported success.
  Escaping is now done by a helper that returns a complete JSON string
  literal, quotes included, so a site that forgets to call it breaks on every
  input rather than only on a rare one. The writer also stopped swallowing
  `IOException`, which had let a failed write leave a truncated file behind
  while `analyzeHeadless` still exited successfully
- **#85** — the lifting script is compiled on every push. Ghidra compiles it at
  lift time, so an error in it was never a build failure — it was a lift that
  produced nothing, reported as a missing output because `analyzeHeadless`
  exits 0 whether or not its script compiled, with the compiler's diagnostic
  buried in the captured process output. `assets/lifters/ghidra/compile-check.sh`, also
  reachable as `just compile-check`, does the same check locally in about two
  seconds instead of a Ghidra round trip
- **#84** — the lifter's README states what a `--script` replacement has to
  satisfy. Four things, two of which are not guessable: the file must be named
  after its public class, and it must escape the names it embeds. It also says
  plainly that `--script` is not a sandbox — the script runs inside Ghidra with
  everything Ghidra can reach
- **#83** — `lift` reads back what it wrote before calling the lift a success.
  A lifting script can write bytes, return normally, and leave behind a file
  nothing can parse; `analyzeHeadless` exits 0 either way, so that used to be a
  successful lift and the failure surfaced at `extract`, as a parse error
  naming a line and column in a file the reader had never seen. The check sits
  in `LifterBuilder::build`, so it covers a script supplied with `--script` —
  arbitrary Java that oinkie never inspects — and any lifter added later,
  without its author having to remember. The error names the binary that was
  lifted, not only the JSON. Related: `lift` and `extract` no longer print
  "completed" on a run that failed
- **#78** — `oinkie mcp` serves oinkie over the Model Context Protocol, on
  stdin and stdout, so an agent can drive the birthmark pipeline directly. This
  release carries the scaffold and one tool, `oinkie_info`, which reports the
  birthmark types, the algorithms and the shapes they operate on, every
  canonical `{birthmark}-{algorithm}` analysis name, the pairing strategies and
  the aggregators — all generated from the same code that parses those names,
  so the list cannot drift from what is accepted. Lifting is deliberately not
  exposed: it runs a whole decompiler process per binary, and a replacement
  script is arbitrary code. The subcommand is behind the `mcp` cargo feature,
  as `gencomp` is, and the released binaries are built with it
- **#80** — the MCP server confines what it will touch. `oinkie mcp --root
  DIRECTORY`, repeatable and defaulting to the working directory, bounds every
  path a tool is handed, input and output alike; anything resolving outside is
  refused with a message naming the directories that are allowed. The paths a
  tool receives are written by a language model rather than by the person
  running it, which the rest of oinkie was never built to assume. A `..`
  component is refused outright rather than resolved, and the existing part of
  a path is canonicalized, so a symlink pointing out of a root does not get
  through either. `oinkie_reaggregate` arrives with it: it recomputes the score
  for every pair in a directory of element-wise CSVs under a different
  aggregator, without comparing anything again
- **#79** — the MCP server compares. `oinkie_run` takes lifted programs and
  reports how similar each pair is, which is the whole question in one call;
  `oinkie_extract` writes birthmarks and `oinkie_compare` scores them, for
  trying several algorithms without re-reading the programs. Each takes its
  vocabulary as names `oinkie_info` lists, and a name the library refuses comes
  back in the library's own words — `op-seq-euclidean` is answered with "use
  op-freq-euclidean" rather than a generic rejection. A destination directory
  is optional and, when given, is written in the same shape `oinkie run -d`
  produces, so it can be handed straight back to `oinkie_reaggregate`. Work
  runs off the async runtime, and a request for more than 500 pairs is refused
  before anything is read rather than after — `all-and-self` is quadratic, and
  a model handed a directory will pass all of it
- **#81** — the MCP server is documented. `cli/mcp/README.md` covers
  configuring a client, the five tools, `--root`, and why lifting is not among
  them; the same is on the site under Usage, and `cli/README.md` carries the
  subcommand's own help. Both container images are now built with the feature,
  so either is an MCP server as it stands — point clients at `light`, which has
  no Ghidra to carry, and remember `-i` without `-t`, since a TTY breaks the
  JSON-RPC framing
